objectives: Apply standard precautions using task-risk-based PPE.
Apply and keep visible the precaution level in force.

items.text: Standard precautions apply to all patients; transmission-based precautions are added as the unit's policy directs.
Choose PPE from the task risk; put it on before the task and remove it in the order and place set by policy, then perform hand hygiene.
Respiratory hygiene and cough etiquette; safe injection and sharps practice; cleaning and disinfection of shared equipment; safe handling of linen and waste.
Hand hygiene means cleaning the hands with soap and water, with an alcohol-based hand rub, or (for surgery) with surgical hand antisepsis.
Alcohol-based hand rub contains ethyl alcohol, is a flammable liquid and must be stored and dispensed in line with local fire-safety rules.

CDC's core practices page gives six hand-hygiene moments: immediately before touching a patient; before an aseptic task or handling an invasive device; before moving from a soiled body site to a clean one on the same patient; after touching a patient or their immediate environment; after contact with blood, body fluids or contaminated surfaces; and immediately after glove removal. Soap and water are called for when hands are visibly soiled; an alcohol-based hand rub is otherwise generally preferred, and supplies should be readily accessible wherever care is delivered.
The precaution level for each patient is set by infection-prevention policy.

The CDC/HICPAC guideline describes three transmission-based precaution categories, used in addition to standard precautions: Contact Precautions (gown and gloves for interactions that may touch the patient or their environment; a single room is preferred) for organisms spread by direct or indirect contact; Droplet Precautions (a mask for close contact, generally donned on room entry; no special air handling needed) for pathogens spread through close respiratory or mucous-membrane contact; and Airborne Precautions (a mask or respirator per the disease-specific recommendation, donned before room entry; an airborne infection isolation room is preferred) for pathogens that remain infectious over long distances in the air. Which organisms require which category, and the exact signage and placement, follow the unit's infection-prevention policy.

Before a task, assess the exposure risk to choose PPE: wear gloves whenever contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin or contaminated equipment can reasonably be anticipated; wear a task-appropriate gown if soiling from fluids is possible; add eye protection with a mask or face shield if splashes or sprays are possible. PPE is secondary to administrative and engineering controls, not a substitute for them.

CDC's core practices call for identifying and monitoring adherence to infection-prevention practices, giving prompt and regular feedback to staff and facility leadership, training the staff who monitor to use standardised tools and definitions, and monitoring facility infections using surveillance data to detect transmission; monitoring measures should be tailored to the care provided and the population served.
Donning and doffing sequences follow the unit's approved procedure.
Record precaution level and exposures per policy.

checklist.text: Choose PPE for the task risk before starting.
Put PPE on before the task and remove it in the order and place your policy sets.
Perform hand hygiene at the moments your policy defines.
Clean and disinfect shared equipment between patients.

gaps: The CDC/HICPAC isolation guideline's disease-specific precaution list (Appendix A - which organism needs which category) and its MDRO-specific chapter were not read; only section III.B's general category descriptions were.
The WHO 2009 hand hygiene guideline was not accessed; the hand-hygiene moments used here are CDC's own six moments, not WHO's five moments, which may differ slightly in wording and grouping.

Exact PPE donning/doffing sequence and hand hygiene technique steps (soap-and-water vs rub technique) are not written; the CDC core practices page states the principles but not a step-by-step sequence.
